PROPOSED COMMITTEE STUDY OF DANGERS OF ARSENIC CONTAMINATION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of the clear medical danger arising out of exposure to arsenic, and in view of the recent revelations of elevated arsenic levels in Cobalt, Red Lake, Moira Lake and Gloucester township in addition to the previously publicized Yellowknife levels, and in light of the failure of the government to establish safe standards for arsenic exposure despite its having knowledge of the dangers for over two years, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House empowers the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to conduct an investigation into the dangers of arsenic contamination and the adequacy of existing standards and efforts to deal with the problem.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the urgency of this matter I ask leave to present a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas):
That this House urges the government to take immediate steps to achieve the implementation of the recommendations made in the report of Dr. Noel Hall on Canadian railway pension plans, dated in September, 1976 and published in January, 1977, particularly the recommendation that all railway pensions be indexed in accordance with the rise in the cost of living, and that special consideration be given to the case of all older railway retirees without delay.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an important matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
Since Canadian researchers are now in a distressing situation because of the government restriction program and the freeze on funds for scientific research and as the federal government policy on that matter has been disastrous so far and that scientific research is, in scope and in nature, the best long term investment, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That the House call upon the federal government to take immediate necessary action so that all agencies concerned, including the National Science Council of Canada, the National Research Council of Canada and the Medical Research Council may benefit from the assistance which is needed by all Canadian researchers to further their scientific work for the betterment of man's condition.

The facts of that situation are these: Ambassador Warren advised me in October of last year of his desire to be moved from Washington at some mutually convenient time. speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may 1 put a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs? On Tuesday, February 8, I requested a report from the minister on the boundary dispute between Canada and the United States. He stated that a series of meetings was held on this matter in Los Angeles and that further meetings will be resuming before the Prime Minister meets with President Carter on Monday next. Since the settlement of this boundary issue involves jurisdiction over the fisheries resources as well as national sovereignty over possible under water oil, gas and mineral development, has the minister any further information to give the House which will ensure there will be no disruption of Canadian fishing activity on the Georges Bank area as of March 1, especially since Ambassador Warren has returned to Canada and I understand he was one of our negotiators on this matter? At the same time will the minister indicate the progress being made by another group of the Department of External Affairs which is working on the maritime boundaries dispute between Canada and the United States.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BOUNDARY DISPUTES RESULTING FROM EXTENSION OF FISHING ZONE-REQUEST FOR PROGRESS REPORT ON SETTLEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the precise way in which the question was phrased, relating to Georges Bank, I could answer briefly that these negotiations are progressing very satisfactorily. That would not tell the total story, however, in the sense that there is also some problem with regard to negotiations on the west coast relative to salmon stocks. This is for the short term or the interim arrangement which we are seeking to obtain for 1977.

The further talks to which the hon. member referred began on Friday last week and continued into Sunday. The members of the Canadian delegation, who returned home, have already reported and will probably be going back again. In other words, it is a continuing negotiating process. It is still my expectation, and I believe I can say it is the hope and expectation of the United States authorities, that we can have in place by March 1 an interim arrangement on fisheries for 1977. The objective of this will be to ensure there is no significant change in traditional fishing patterns. This would be put in place with a view to obtaining a period without difficulty for fishermen in 1977 during which the longer term negotiations on the boundary might take place.

The House resumed, from Wednesday, February 16, 1977, consideration of the motion of Mr. Basford that Bill C-25, to extend the present laws in Canada that proscribe discrimination and that protect the privacy of individuals, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned yesterday certain categories of discrimination which are not covered in the bill before us. I mentioned among other things the "freedom of conscience" which is not provided for as such in the bill in the provisions on religion; I feel this is a much very wider extension of the freedom of any individual to practise the religion of his choice or to decide not to have any religion. I also talked about expanding the provisions in the sexual area to cover homosexuals who are still discriminated against in spite of the fact that we amended the Criminal Code several years ago. I also mentioned other categories like the political beliefs and the social or economic conditions of people.
Today I would like to insist on one area of discrimination which is not mentioned as such in the bill and which, in my humble opinion, should have priority if we consider the political context in this country, its history and its problems: I refer to language. Of course, the bill does mention national or ethnic origin as well as race but, Mr. Speaker, I think that the word "language" should absolutely be included in the bill.
We are all aware, I hope, of the acuteness of the linguistic issue in this country, and I find it absolutely strange and astounding that the bill fails to mention this motive which, for a large part of the population, namely Francophones, constitutes in our view a discriminatory practice which has been investigated in depth, among others by the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) who introduced this bill will have to agree to add this motive, not to lessen the others that are already in the bill, but to recall that, given the number of Francophones in Canada, this problem is of prime importance for French-speaking
3144

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
people. The Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Bicultur-alism has shown to what extent French-speaking people, or Francophones, are discriminated against. For instance, how in the province of Quebec, in spite of the fact that they are in the majority, they are at the bottom of the income scale. I think that by trying to skip this question, which is fundamental for us as well as for a good part of the people, namely Frenchspeaking Canadians, we are not being fair to them in this bill.
To explain my view, Mr. Speaker, I shall refer to clauses 9 and 10, which affect both unions and employers, and see to what extent those clauses, in their present wording, could have spared us, for instance, the crisis which we are now experiencing at Air Canada. Given the wording of these clauses, I do not think that they would have prevented the discrimination suffered by French-speaking Canadians, particularly mechanics in Air Canada's workshops in Montreal.
Here, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to quote some findings from the Official Languages Commissioner's report published two weeks ago and submitted to Air Canada's chairman regarding the situation of Air Canada's French-speaking employees. I am quoting from page 5 of the report: "Although Air Canada has made visible progress, particularly in its eastern region operations, at the moment of our review the situation was generally unacceptable for the corporation's French-speaking employees." English was the almost exclusive working language within the services of the head office and the employees in the eastern region had to use it when communicating with the head office.
The study stressed more particularly the following defects: lack of a dynamic policy promoting the use of French; lack of French working facilities which are essential to employees; deficiency in the recruiting policy and laxism in the staffing of bilingual jobs; lack of bilingual senior officers; insufficient technical training in French; negative attitude of some senior officers with respect to the use of French for operational communications.
Mr. Speaker, after reading this excerpt, I must again say with renewed emphasis to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Bas-ford) and the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) that the recognition of the language as a reason for illicit discrimination should absolutely be included in this bill if we really want to give justice to those groups which the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism considered as the other majority.
So, I repeat that clauses 9 and 10 in their present form have not dealt with the situation which was described by the Official Languages Commissioner and which we all know. I think that this demonstrates most eloquently that, as concerns reasons for discrimination based on language, the bill as drafted falls far short of the present situation.
Clause 14 of the bill provides, I think, an easy way out as it stipulates that refusal, exclusion and expulsion are not discriminatory practices if they are based on a bona fide occupational requirement. This is the pretext always used by Air Canada to justify the exclusion of French-speaking people

from that Crown corporation. If we leave to the employer total discretion to declare when exclusions, refusals or expulsions are based on a bona fide occupational requirement and he is the only one to establish it, I think it is an easy way out of observing the objective of the bill.
Another provision that, I think, should be amended is clause 19 of the bill providing that the cabinet can, in a contract with a third party, demand that the provisions of this bill be observed. I do not understand how this clause 19 gives such discretional powers in a field like this one, as it means that companies contracting with the government will be able, unless otherwise provided, to discriminate and engage in practices that are considered in this bill as contrary to public order and justice.
1 think that clause 19, by not forcing the government to demand that companies contracting with it refrain from discriminatory practices provided in this bill, represents a dilution of principles according to which we believe that nobody in our society should be the victim of a discriminatory practice. Another provision I find quite strange is paragraph 13(2) where, after it is provided in the first part that it is forbidden to communicate telephonically to expose a group of people to hatred, it says that there is no offense when it is done through a broadcasting undertaking. If it is forbidden to expose a certain group to hatred telephonically, I think it should also apply to the use of broadcasting.
The Solicitor General reminds me that we passed a section on that subject in the Criminal Code a few years ago when the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was minister of justice, which is true. But I do not think it is a good legislative approach to stipulate in a bill on discrimination that it does not apply in the case of communications on radio or television and I am convinced that the Solicitor General will agree with me.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind the House that the United States went much further by creating the Commission for Equal Employment Opportunity. Indeed, it is forbidden in the United States to engage in discriminatory practices, not only within the government itself but also in the big corporations to whom the government contracts out. Moreover, they must take what is called "affirmative action", that is dynamic action to compensate and remedy an unacceptable situation. I do not think this bill does as much since it does not stress what the Americans call affirmative action and what I would call dynamic action.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we are wrong in thinking we will solve our problems if we simply go on saying it is forbidden to discriminate against Indians without making it mandatory, as did the United States with the Commission for Equal Employment Opportunity, to establish positive programs to correct the whole situation within a few years.
Finally, I would like to mention that this bill gives too much importance to regulations that the governor in council may make in future. When comparing this bill, especially the second part dealing with privacy, to The Privacy Act adopted in 1974 by the American Congress, we realize that it is much
February 17, 1977

shorter than its American counterpart, mostly due to the fact that we refer too many decisions to the governor in council. Recently, a committee made up of members from all the different parties came to the unanimous conclusion that all too often when civil servants are allowed to enact regulations, they cause abuses and breach the fundamental rights in which we believe.
Finally, in respect of the language problem, it will no doubt be referred in the course of this debate to a provincial statute, namely Quebec's Bill 22, which grants some sort of precedence to the French language in Quebec. My impression is that, in opposition to that act, there will be allegations that it discriminates against the English language in Quebec. In answer I would call attention to clause 15(1) of this legislation, where it is provided that:
It is not a discriminatory practice for a person to adopt or carry out a special program ... designed to prevent disadvantages that are likely to be suffered by, or to eliminate ... disadvantages that are suffered by, any group ...
My intention is not to discuss here the pros and cons of Bill 22, this would be irrelevant anyway. I would simply submit the following reflection to my hon. colleagues: French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec would be quite happy if they were granted in their provinces the same rights that are recognized under Bill 22 to the English-speaking minority in Quebec.
I simply want to remind them that no group of Frenchspeaking Canadians outside the province of Quebec enjoys the same rights as those recognized through Bill 22 to the Englishspeaking minority in Quebec. One must wonder how we can speak of equal and symmetrical measures when 98 per cent of people in North America use the English language currently with a French-speaking minority of about 2 per cent. If one thinks that it is the English language that is threatened in Canada and in North America where 98 per cent of the people use it, I would say that the blindest of all is he who does not want to see.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, some of the comments which come to my mind at this stage of debate on this bill. I hope that in committee each of us will be able to suggest amendments to strengthen the bill so that the basic intent of this legislation will be the primacy of the individual, the primacy of the human being over institutions, which should be our first concern, I believe. This purpose could be better served than in the present bill, which of course represents a step toward the improvement of the situation, but which does not go far enough, in my opinion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity of debating what I consider to be a very important bill. I am pleased that my hon. friend from Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) set the tone of the debate by indicating that there are problems which must be attended to, hopefully by way of amendments to the bill, to ensure the emergence of satisfactory legislation which at present is not satisfactory.
Canadian Human Rights
My hon. friend for Matane (Mr. De Bane) has indicated that there are some problems with respect to the "hate message" provision. He wondered, as I do, why broadcasting is an exception. I will have something to say about that, as well as about the awarding of contracts under, I believe, clause 19 and about the protection of personal information.
I think the debate on this bill is timely. I become a little dismayed when I pick up newspapers across the country and read that we have been relatively silent at the federal level about the verbal and physical assault and harassments which the visible minority in particular have been experiencing in the past few years. Therefore, it is about time we in this House realized that there is a role we can play, an interest that must be shown and a concern that should be registered. That is why, if I seem to be a little off target with respect to this bill, Mr. Speaker, you will understand because I want to bring forward some thoughts that I have, in the very short time at my disposal, in regard to what is happening in Canada and what I think Canada should be all about.
Since my election to the House of Commons I have had the opportunity on many occasions to travel the width and breadth of this land. Because of this opportunity I have been reminded continually of the greatness of this country, not so much because of its size but because of its way of life which has evolved and continues to evolve through the talents and cultures of peoples from various backgrounds.
In Canada we are overcome by the consciousness of the enormous task that needs doing. We all know that Canada takes in the northern half of the North American continent, involving a huge mass of real estate within which lies some of the world's richest resources. We have the responsibility, first, of maintaining our ownership and, second, of developing these resources for the benefit of mankind. This responsibility and development is a challenge for all Canadians regardless of race, creed or colour. This is a challenge of enormous implications, and to meet this challenge all people need, and deserve, the understanding and accord of each other and the assistance of enlightened government policy.
We are a nation of some 22 million people living together, involving various cultures, lands and heritages, all working together in dedication and with common purpose, the ultimate aim being a greater Canada in which all can share its wealth through equality of opportunity. Let me remind you, Mr. Speaker, that statesmen, politicians and economists are only incidental in the pursuit of the building of Canada. It is the people who will make or break this nation's life. What of its people? I am reminded of the comments of a citizenship judge who said:
This nation has been enriched by the loyalty and sacrifice of persons who have come from many lands, heritages and traditions. To each this nation has given a chance to live and grow and share in the Commonwealth. From each Canada has accepted the gifts of different cultures and made them into an enduring heritage from sea to sea. This rich heritage is yours, as it is mine, because we are Canadians.
80008-61 Vi

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
The hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) in a speech some time ago paraphrased a sentiment which I thought was put so beautifully. I should like to say that I maintain that our country has been enriched by the beautiful and noble culture of the first Canadians; by the gaiety and passion of the French Canadians; by the measured dignity of the Anglo-Saxons; by the stern efficiency of the Teutonic races; by the vivid tones of the Celts; by the moving processional of 1,000 years by the Baltic peoples; by the diligence of the Italian community; by the beauty and age-old mystic of Asia and Africa; and by the grandeur and pathos of the Jewish pilgrims.
As Canadians, we have rejoiced in and have been strengthened by all of these different and varied qualities of enrichment. No Canadian race, no melting pot, no fashioning all into one mould, but, rather, we are pursuing the attainment of an identity which is based on intelligence, tolerance and decent, neighbourly attitudes. We are in the midst of the great Canadian experiment, that is to say, freedom to pursue our legitimate aspirations and evolving further: equality of opportunity; greater appreciation of different cultures, heritage and customs; and last but not least, bringing about racial accord.
In light of the fact that we are still in the midst of this great Canadian experiment, and because some are not even aware of the same, it is necessary from time to time to reflect again on what it hopes to accomplish. When I speak of the great Canadian experiment, I am speaking about a very simple principle which is the elimination of inter-group prejudices which disfigure and distort religious, business, social and political relations, with a view to the establishment of a social order in which the religious ideals of government and justice shall become the standards of human relationships.
This legislation gives us an opportunity to dedicate ourselves as individuals to the basic ideals of respect for people and human rights, which are essential to our way of life and, further, to dramatize the practical things which people can do to promote understanding and realization of these ideals at the federal level, thus giving leadership to all Canadians on human relations. Although there has been considerable improvement in attitudes, one must admit there are still too many who have kept, and do keep, people down or let them stay down by using powers either openly or subtly in discriminatory ways. For centuries many have fought for equality and although, as I have said, things have improved, it seems to me we still have work ahead of us. Indeed there has been progress, but nevertheless in Canada and throughout the world there still remains a degree of social and economic injustice based on colour, religion, language and sex.
The special needs and requests, and even demands, of those affected by discrimination because of colour, religion, language or sex are treated with apathy and indifference by too many people, such as those in positions of power, including members sitting in this chamber. There can be no doubt that the legitimate aspirations of these people to achieve recognition or redress are at times ignored completely, or even met with outright hostility. Accordingly, notwithstanding improve-

ment, there is a backlog of social and economic problems that can no longer be ignored if for no other reason than people have refused to remain patient in the face of injustice or settle for token measures that placate but do not remedy.
Many of us have been the victim of racial discrimination and have suffered grinding poverty and eventual degradation, a serious disability in facing the world. People of colour, in particular, have faced these horrible odds and obstacles and have kept alive their traditions and hopes notwithstanding. It seems to me that all the various stigmas and restrictions imposed on people, whether consciously or unconsciously, whether derived from colour, form of religious worship, degree of education, language, sex, and all the rest, are simply impediments to the advancement and development of an expanding society.
The tragedy in Canada is not only that many of those classed as visible minorities have not been completely accepted or recognized in a white society, but as well our human resources, a priceless social asset, are not permitted to make or are restricted from making a maximum contribution to Canadian society. No one in Canada should have to limit themselves socially, politically, culturally or economically. Yet by the actions of some, whether consciously or not, many of our people have been limited.
As a member of the Senate and House of Commons Joint Committee on Immigration, I travelled across this country and noticed that there still remains in varying degrees and in different locations in Canada racial and religious discrimination. Let me assure hon. members that despicable hate letters and hate messages are still around, and insidious social discrimination continues to rear its ugly head. But what is most important, I found that the vast majority of Canadians find these attitudes and actions despicable, distasteful, not wanted and not needed, which to me is certainly very encouraging.
Myths and untruths were prominent during these hearings, but the committee, after deliberation subsequent to the hearings, attacked many if not all of the myths and certainly emphasized truths. For example, quoting from the report of the joint committee, section 20 thereof:
A persistent theme of submissions, hostile to immigration, was the view that immigrants crowded cities, exacerbating housing shortages, increasing the crime rate, bringing infectious diseases, taxing the welfare rolls and government services and causing unemployment by taking jobs from Canadians.
In this regard the committee reached the following conclusion:
The committee recognizes that all these problems are faced by rapidly growing cities but concluded they are caused by economic, social and cultural dynamism of cities and their attractiveness to Canadians and immigrants alike.
The committee further concluded:
Canadians worried about the quality of life in our cities should took elsewhere than to sharply reduced immigration for a solution to the problems of city living.
I would refer again to the report. Section 22 continues:
Similar misconceptions also abound regarding the impact of immigration on social services and benefits and health care. None of the testimony supported
February 17, 1977

with facts the popular notion that newcomers are using these services more than the native-born. If anything, the committee has the impression that the use of such services by immigrants falls below the national average for the obvious reason that many come from countries where such services are traditionally provided by the family. Indeed, it would appear that interprovincial and rural to urban migrants make greater use of government support than persons from abroad.
Section 23 has an interesting conclusion, and I quote:
Nor do immigrants participate less actively in the work force than long-term residents.
Another myth was exploded, and in this regard I would refer to section 24 which reads in part as follows:
Some submissions contained allegations that immigrants, especially the nonwhite, contribute proportionately to the crime rate-
Expert testimony did not support this charge, and I emphasize that. It continues:
-and in a study prepared for the ministry of the Solicitor General of Canada in 1974 statistics indicated that the crime rate for immigrants was approximately one-half that for native-born Canadians.
Another section which I believe is worthy of your consideration is section 26, which reads:
The committee recognizes that it has been through the contributions and efforts of successive generations of immigrants that Canada has grown to be the relatively secure, prosperous and satisfying place it is. About four million immigrants have come to Canada since World War II. Their skills, their energies and their enthusiasm have added immeasurably to every facet of Canadian life and have created a vibrant multicultural mosaic. The committee firmly believe that the settlement of post-war immigrants alongside the founding cultures is one of the most positive chapters in Canada's post-war history. It looks to immigration to continue to contribute to the economic, cultural and social well-being of the country.
I would like to read another commendable section in the report, section 39, which reads as follows:
There is a danger of creating second-class citizens of many foreign-bom who have made their homes in Canada. It is evident that the ability of newcomers to adapt readily and successfully to Canadian life is in large part contingent on the esteem in which they are held by their chosen communities and on the existence of non-discriminatory treatment in employment, housing and services. The committee makes this assertion in the confident belief that the majority of the Canadian people are tolerant and generous, and not prepared to condone racial hostility and discrimination.
The committee also reported, in effect, that Canada has become to a large extent a multicultural and multiracial society, and it further stated that in order to promote intergroup understanding the committee recommends public and school education as well as legislative action to protect Canadians and immigrants alike from racial and ethnic discrimination. This society of ours, of course, must become greater, and in order to achieve the ultimate in greatness we must be prepared to understand that in our diversity lies a tremendous asset and that intolerance, injustice, discrimination and hate can only bring us to ruin.
As Thomas Curtis Clarke stated: "Let us no more be true to boasted race or clan but to the highest dream, the brotherhood of man". Will you allow me, Mr. Speaker, to quote Stephen Vincent Benet who said:
Grant us brotherhood not only this day but for all our years. A brotherhood not of words but of acts and deeds. We are all children of the earth; grant us that simple knowledge. If our brothers are oppressed, then we are oppressed; if they hunger, we hunger; if their freedom is taken away, our freedom is not secure.
Canadian Human Rights
Canadians must stand against prejudice, Canadians must stand for justice, and they must stand for equal opportunity for all. We as Canadians, have, I remind the House, a commitment to that end. Since December 10, 1940, when the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, there has been an increasing awareness in many countries of the need for enactment of domestic laws and the creation of internal mechanisms to deal with discrimination. In this regard, all provinces have enacted statutes respecting human rights and I believe all those statutes have provisions for the establishment of a human rights commission. Of course, the provinces have taken the lead in this field because discriminatory practices have tended to be more prevalent in matters under provincial jurisdiction in the areas of employment,, accommodation and services, and because so many more Canadians are involved with matters under provincial jurisdiction.
What about the federal government? At present the federal government and its existing anti-discrimination provisions, federal statutes and regulations, are fragmentary. For example, within the Canada Labour Code, which deals with fair employment practices, certain provisions apply to the employment practices of organizations such as banks, railways, etc., under the jurisdiction of parliament, but do not include employment by the Crown in right of Canada, which is certainly unacceptable. I hope that will be rectified now.
I mentioned taped messages earlier which in my view, reflecting on the arsenal of hatred involved in which the taped voice is included, spilling forth malice and tolerance on the telephone, is the most insidious. After discussion with the provinces, and particularly with the attorney general of the province of Ontario, we now have a provision within this act regarding hate messages. But, as I pointed out earlier, it should include broadcasting. I hope that my colleagues on both sides of the House will ensure that this provision is accepted. The federal government is involved with a multicultural society; let us make no mistake about that. Although we do have much legislation which attempts to protect human rights and the dignity of man, more is needed. In asking for more, it is sad to reflect that our society is so warped that it continually needs to introduce legislation to bring about racial accord. Accordingly, a Canadian human rights act was introduced. The purpose of this bill is to prohibit discrimination in all matters within federal jurisdiction on the grounds of race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, etc. The bill also provides for a Canadian human rights commission at the federal level.
Because of this act there will be an over-all body of law at the federal level to which persons may resort when they consider themselves harmed by the discriminatory practice of organizations, Crown corporations or persons whose activities fall within the legislative authority of parliament. As well, there will be legislation providing for the establishment of standards on the basis of which personal information and government records are accurate, accessible to the individual, and used only for authorized purposes. When we look at this

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
matter of the protection of personal information, we find that part of the preamble of Bill C-25 states that:
The privacy of individuals should be protected to the greatest extent consistent with public order and well-being.
Compared to the universal declaration of rights section dealing with privacy, this is vague, weak and limited. Clause 52 and the noble sentiments of the preamble sound good. However, with the exceptions outlined in clauses 53, 54, 55 and 62(l)(d), all of clause 52 is made, or can be made, potentially useless since records can be withheld from the proposed information bank, or only partially listed at the discretion of any minister in charge of an information bank. Accordingly, the intent of clause 52 is completely emasculated and becomes useless. The whole section on privacy is like a game of definitions in which the individual has most of his right to information to lose. For instance, subclause 52(2) provides that individuals must be consulted before records are made available for any non-derivative use.
Note, however, that in defining "derivative use" the legislation hinges it upon the minister's opinion, that is, a derivative use is one that in the opinion of the minister is consistent with the use for which the record was compiled. This, in effect, means any use, since we all know that word games are the easiest to play.
Another instance is clause 55 which, in effect, is a blanket discretionary clause cloaked in terms relating to public benefit and the cost of applying the clauses or provisions. Any provision will not apply if the minister feels that the public benefits derived from the application of those provisions will be outweighed by the costs. This clause alone could reduce the information available to strictly trivial information collected about an individual. The cost of many rights in monetary terms may outweigh the public benefit, but this does not mean we should not be willing to bear that extra cost. I read somewhere that this clause of the bill was rewritten 15 times. I am sure that was to make certain that the bill was couched in such terms that the government would not have to reveal anything it did not wish to reveal, while at the same time appearing to have a comprehensive personal information policy.
If this legislation is passed as it stands, people will not have access to many records because they will not be listed in the government index which supposedly is compiled to inform us and aid us in obtaining information. People will not be able to ascertain accurately to what uses those records have been put since knowledge of the existence of secret records and partially listed records will be beyond the access of the individual. Of course, even if a record is available, one could never be sure that it is complete since the minister has the discretion to restrict the information published. The principle behind these exemptions seems a little absurd because, in effect, they counteract the underlying purpose of this part by preventing an individual from seeing information collected about himself on herself. In short, the protection of personal information is very inadequate and this part should be scrapped completely and rewritten.
Another major objection to the bill is that there is no explicit clause dealing with the manner in which government contracts will be awarded, that is, a contract compliance provision. Granted, clause 19 states that the governor in council may-which is permissive-make regulations with respect to this matter, but it is not clearly and effectively delineated and it is too important to be stuck away in the regulations. In my view, the legislation should be rewritten and the commission specifically empowered to give certificates of compliance to all prospective bidders on government contracts. For example, every department or agency awarding contracts for construction, alteration or repair of public works must employ direct methods of ensuring that minority group persons are employed to a significant degree on all such projects-and this goal must apply wherever public funds are expended.
The obligation thus placed on an employer to provide employment opportunity requires more than his willingness not to discriminate, more than a posture of neutrality. For this reason compliance laws, is most cases, are accompanied by affirmative action programs. I could go on with respect to that matter, Mr. Speaker, but my time is running out and I did promise to conclude very shortly.
In any event, by a direct and visible effort we are attempting to support the original objectives of the United Nations proposed decade programs which are to promote human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, colour, descent, national or ethnic orgin, especially by eradicating racial prejudice, racism and racial discrimination; to arrest any expansion of racist policies; to eliminate the persistence of racist policies and to counteract the emergence of racist policies and to counteract the emergence of alliances based on mutual espousal of racism and racial discrimination; to resist any policy and practices which lead to the strengthening of the racist regime and which contribute to the sustaining of racism and racial discrimination; to identify, isolate and dispel the fallacious and mythical beliefs, policies and practices which contribute to racism and racial discrimination; and to eliminate racist regimes.
The cancerous sore of racism, prejudice and discrimination which devours reasoning, love, compassion and tolerance is a problem for which education alone in the schools, the churches and the home is not enough, and therefore calls for other treatment. In this regard I place emphasis on the political scalpel-in other words, legislation-which can ensure that all of us in this multicultural society will have a meaningful future. It seems to me that many of us believe that the winds of change affect underdeveloped countries only, but I point out that in Canada also there is a wind affecting the attitude of all peoples and groups in their day-to-day relationships. Attitudes are affecting the thinking of the United Nations, the dogma of churches, the decisions of courts and the legislative programs of governments. There is a new social awareness and there are new attitudes calling for action.
I am not saying that the government should assure the survival of every ethnic group, but I am stressing that it should

February 17, 1977

give everyone a reasonable opportunity to survive by seeing to it that the necessary climate for survival is in effect and is maintained. Such action must result in helping to assure that there will be an equal place in all aspects of life in this country for everyone without regard to race, origin or religion, failing which I am immediately reminded of a comment made by a former United States secretary of state when speaking about the American administration. He said:
If no one will listen, the lack of communication will cause more frustration and fear, and fear leads to hate and hate leads to violence.
I am pleased to have an opportunity to become involved with this bill. I would like to see its quick passage so that we can determine how best to contrive methods to make the bill even more meaningful. I am particularly interested in the hate message aspect of the bill because we will need the co-operation and the expertise of Bell Canada. I hope we are making some significant strides in order to see that there will be no hold-up, when this bill is passed, with respect to the installation of the necessary equipment to reduce, if not eliminate, hate messages.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on second reading of Bill C-25, legislation to extend the present laws in Canada which prohibit discrimination and which protect the privacy of individuals. It is also known by its short title, the Canadian Human Rights Act. At the beginning of my remarks I would like to commend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) for bringing forward this legislation and also to express our appreciation to the Advisory Council on the Status of Women and to all other associations for their contributions to this bill.
Canadians have waited a long time for this legislation in the federal field, not only because of their personal interest and concern about civil liberties and Canada's commitment to human rights declarations and covenants at the United Nations but also because the federal government has been lagging behind provincial human rights legislation. It is timely that we in this House enact the provisions of this human rights bill, especially during this period known as the decade for action, to combat racism and racial discrimination, a program officially launched by a special United Nations General Assembly on December 10, 1973. Canada supported the adoption of this UN program, and it is only proper that the federal government has ratified the human rights convenants and conventions and continues to bring in legislation to help eradicate discrimination and racism, to increase understanding between the various groups which make up the multicultural and pluralistic society of this country and to promote respect for the human rights and fundamental freedoms of people both within our country and universally.
That is why I warmly welcome the purpose of this legislation, which is that every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she wishes to have, consistent with their duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour,
Canadian Human Rights
religion, age, sex or marital status, a conviction which has been pardoned, or by discriminatory employment practices based on physical handicap.
The bill is also intended to protect the privacy of individuals to the greatest extent consistent with public order and wellbeing. This bill, therefore, upholds the universally acknowledged fundamental principles of inherent dignity and equal rights to all members of the human race, the same spirit that this House unanimously has demonstrated during the past year or two in voicing its concern wherever human rights have been violated.
However, to be effective and of benefit, human rights legislation must be put into practice and really enforced. The high-minded human rights principles embodied in the constitution of the Weimar republic did not prevent Hitler manipulating those very principles to secure the power to abolish the principles, and today, alas, the human rights principles in the constitutions of many countries are ineffective because they are not enforced. We welcome, therefore, this Canadian human rights bill because of the comprehensive guarantees against infringement of many basic egalitarian rights and the provision of measures to enforce those rights.
Prior to this bill before us today there was only limited protection of egalitarian rights at the federal level in specific areas such as employment practices, fair wages, housing and immigration. Additional protection for federal employees was offered by setting up the anti-discrimination branch of the Public Service Commission and the Public Service Commission appeals branch. However, apparently these protective measures were inadequate and the proposed prohibitions in this bill against discriminatory conduct will apply to all federal departments and agencies and any business or industry under federal responsibility. However, I am puzzled by the absence in the schedule of this bill of Crown corporations such as Air Canada and the CNR. I hope that further speeches on the bill, and the minister's reply, especially at committee stage, will provide answers why these and other questions have been exempted from the schedule.
This bill is timely because it will help defuse racial tensions to which hon. members have already referred and which seem to be increasing in our country. We also welcome the provision which prohibits discrimination on the grounds of sex and marital status, especially the proposal to require equal pay for work of equal value. Above all, the strength of this proposed legislation lies in the provision of enforcement by an independent human rights commission, responsible only to parliament, with wide powers to set up tribunals and to impose financial penalties. To enable this commission to be really effective and progressive, adequate funds must be provided for research and public education, and the government-especially the minister-should make sure that all sectors of our society are represented.
In our complex society which is often overgoverned and frustrated by bureaucratic red tape there is a need to protect

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
individual privacy and prevent administrative misuse of personal files in government information banks. We must also give our citizens unfettered access to their personal files and the opportunity to propose corrections where errors exist. The proposal in Bill C-25 to establish the position of a privacy commissioner to review any complaint by any individual that he or she is being denied rights under the act makes some progress in meeting the need of citizens who fear that information about them is incorrect or misused.
This bill does not cover everything in the field of human rights. We must admit, however, that it is a step in the right direction and, indeed, an improvement over previous attempts to bring forth human rights legislation in the federal field. Though we do not have a utopia in this country, a parliamentary committee will study the bill clause by clause and interested ethnic groups and civil liberties experts will have every opportunity to study it.
It is urgent, in our present constitutional and national unity crisis, to develop a comprehensive, constitutionally entrenched Canadian charter of human rights. Many people have voiced the same opinion. One such charter, which I believe should be recommended reading material for those studying the bill, was produced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when as minister of justice he inspired many Canadians and the delegates at the 1968 federal-provincial constitutional conference. At that meeting he proposed a constitutionally entrenched bill of human rights for Canada guaranteeing the fundamental freedoms of the individual and equal rights for all Canadians-namely, political, legal, egalitarian, economic and linguistic. I should like to quote from a document entitled "A Canadian Charter of Human Rights", especially the section on linguistic rights, page 27, which reads as follows:
Education-guaranteeing the right of the individual to education in institutions using as a medium of instruction the official language of his choice.
The hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane) made some remarks about linguistic rights. I want to reiterate that all of us have heard complaints that specific sections of Quebec's official language act do not comply with either the spirit or letter of the Canadian charter of human rights nor the international conventions, covenants and declaration on human rights which Canada has thus far ratified. I therefore appeal to the Minister of Justice, often regarded as our chief ombudsman, to examine these complaints and come to the assistance of those sectors of the Quebec population-especially the parents and children of minority ethnic groups-who feel that their linguistic rights in education have been abrogated.
Another complaint to which we should give our attention is the under-representation in parliament and federal agencies as well as the underutilization in industry, especially at senior executive levels, of the skills, talents and experience of members of the minority ethnic groups in Canada. Some progress in this matter has been made, especially in recent years, but more remains to be done to level out the vertical mosaic.
There should be no need for any Canadian to become culturally assimilated or to change the family name in order to obtain a high position in government or industry. I believe the

federal government's total commitment to multiculturalism and human rights will lead to harmonious relations in Canada and contribute immensely to national unity which we must strengthen and pass on, enhanced, to future generations.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has already pointed out on behalf of this party, we welcome this bill for the good that is in it. We hope that the portions that are not satisfactory will be corrected or improved when the bill gets to the standing committee. In particular, we welcome the declaration of equality of rights amongst all Canadians and the declaration that certain things which are identified as discrimination are to be prohibited. The section of the bill that disappoints us is that having to do with the privacy commission. As I have said, the hon. member for Greenwood has already stated our position with regard to that portion of the bill.
I propose to address my few remarks in this debate exclusively to one aspect of the bill and I hope to say a few things that are specific within that context. I am sure that we all welcome the attempt of this legislation to take us further down the road in terms of equality between men and women in Canada. Other speakers have paid their tributes to those who have participated in the production of this bill. I should like to add to those who have been named such persons as the late Agnes MacPhail, the Hon. Therese Casgrain and others of bygone decades who did their best to establish women's rights in this country. We are grateful to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, which was chaired by Mrs. Florence Bird, and we are appreciative of the work done by the Advisory Committee on the Status of Women and also by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women.
Establishing this kind of equality is a slow process and we all recognize that there are problems. As I have already indicated, however, I wish to speak of a few things in relation to the equality of women with men which have not yet been achieved. As a matter of fact, I am going to get even narrower in my interest than I have suggested. One could talk about the differences that exist between men and women in rates of pay, despite our equal pay legislation; one could talk about the discrimination that still exists in employment; one could talk about the particular problems that face women who are single parents-all those things where we may declare the rights are equal. But there are countries in other parts of the world who give the answer that the constitution says everybody is equal when it really is not so. My point is, it is not enough to say that women's rights are equal with men's rights, although it is good to say it. It is worth while to have that declaration in this bill, but my point is, we must not stop there.
I said 1 would limit my remarks to the question of the equality of women, and I will narrow them still further. It will not surprise hon. members to know that I am concerned about inequalities in the field of pensions. First, I mention the Canada Pension Plan. The government, in this very session,
February 17, 1977

plans to bring in amendments to the Canada Pension Plan, amendments which it says are to extend to women rights which now apply to men. I point out that no matter how much one says that those pension provisions are open to either sex, the fact is that most men in their working years are in the Canada Pension Plan, but a large number of women are not. Until we recognize that a woman's contribution in the home is just as much a part of the production of goods and services as the work any person does in an office or factory, we will not establish equality. You can say all you want about the Canada Pension Plan being equally open to all, in the sense that any employee, male or female, contributes to and participates in the plan, but the fact is that by far the largest number of persons between the ages of 18 and 65 who are not in the Canada Pension Plan are women. I suggest, in practical terms, that is a case of gross inequality.
Let me draw a parallel. Membership of the House of Commons is equally open to men and women, but in the 110 years in which the Canadian House of Commons has existed, about 3,000 men have been elected to this place, but only 28 women. Sir, there is equality in the sense that men and women have equal rights to become members of this House, but in practice it does not work that way.
Mir. Woolliams: It sure does not.

speechtext: Incidentally, the statistic I mentioned of 28 women having been elected to this place in 110 years ought to shame us. I heard a comment, but I did not catch it.
