speechtext: Most of the women were elected fairly recently.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Yes. Actually, all 28 women have been elected in the last 50 years. In the previous 50 or 60 years none was elected. During the past 110 years we have had 30 elections; therefore, on the average we have not elected even one woman per election. The Canada Elections Act says that everybody 18 years old and over can run for parliament. The human rights bill says that we are all equal. Yet unless something else is done, that equality will not exist.
Women have equal rights with men for the top posts in the public service, private industry, the boards of directors of banks, and so on. But how many women ever make it there? It is a miracle if women ever make it in certain professions. On the other hand, other professions seem to be left primarily to women. I do not expect the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to correct all this in this bill, but I urge that it is not enough just to declare equal rights. Other things must be done.
I wanted to deal specifically with pension matters and I began by talking about the Canada Pension Plan. That, ostensibly, is legislation applying equally to men and women. It is true that under the law a man who dies leaves certain rights to his surviving widow, and the woman contributor who dies leaves the same rights to her surviving husband. That is supposed to be equality. But that equality is gained on death.
Canadian Human Rights
Unfortunately, a woman's chance for participating in the Canada Pension Plan during her lifetime is denied, is limited, not by law but by the structure of our society. Those who designed the Canada Pension Plan failed to make provision for housewives or homemaker spouses, as we sometimes call them, to obtain pension benefits equivalent to benefits obtainable outside the home. That is a clear denial of equal rights.
I move to another pension area and suggest that some of the things one could say about pensions in the public service and pensions in the private sector can also be said about the provisions we make for widows. I know that this is a little speech I often make in this House. Hon. members have heard me say this a good many times, and I do not apologize for it. You can only get some things done around this place by repeating what you have to say time and again.
The pension system in the public service and private industry is for the most part based on the idea that the husband is the contributor; therefore, when it is time to retire and the husband and wife are both alive, they get 100 per cent of the pension-the pension which has been earned from employment either in the public or private sector. So all is well; they have both contributed in their ways, made their lives together and when they retire and both are alive they get the full pension. If the wife dies first, the husband's pension carries on at 100 per cent. But if the husband dies first, in most cases the widow's pension carries on but only at 50 per cent. In a few cases 60 per cent, although in some cases it is less than 50 per cent or there is no widow's pension at all. You cannot contend with success that there is equality in pensions paid either in the public sector or the private sector when such situations exist. Sir, I am not so naive as to think that the Minister of Justice can with the passage of this bill do away with all those inequalities, although I can tell you that there are Canadians out there who have heard of this bill and are hoping it will pass and bring about greater equality as between men and women so that some inequalities which work to the detriment of women in the field of pensions will be corrected.
I move to another topic with which many are familiar, that of widows of public service personnel, in which I include personnel of the RCMP and the Canadian armed forces. If the marriage took place after the husband retired from employment in the public service or any of the other services I mentioned, there is no pension for the widow. As long as the marriage took place before retirement, she can get a pension. Sir, this bill says that there is to be no discrimination, no difference on the basis of marital status. I do not know how one can say that this is being practiced if pension status depends upon the date of marriage. I have already objected to the inequality which results from widows getting only 50 per cent pensions when they ought to get a 100 per cent pension. Unfair though the payment of a 50 per cent pension to widows may be, I point out that some widows get no pension at all because their marriage did not take place before the magic date required under the law.
I refer also to veterans' widows, to the case in which the pension to the widow is based upon the level of the veteran's
3152

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
pension. The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) a moment ago referred to the schedule to the bill. I notice that the Canadian Pension Commission is in the schedule to the bill and is listed as one of the entities which is supposed to determine these matters under this law. This law states that there is to be equality. However, a veteran who is on a disability pension in some cases leaves a widow with a pension and in some cases leaves a widow without a pension.
I am very familiar with how these pensions plans were built up; I know the pension theory that is involved in them. In this legislation we are trying to establish a new concept. It is not brand new; it has been pushed for decades. We have been making progress in this field but we still have not got to anything that can be called real equality in the pension field.
I seem to be listing all kinds of pensions where there are these inequalities. We at least have one where there is equality-old age security. A man or woman gets the pension because he or she meets the age requirement and the residence requirement. There is no question about marital status. This bill has something to say about discriminating against age, but it makes the exception that you do not have to pay a pension to everybody. It is perfectly proper to put down an age at which pensions are payable. Apart from that, there are gross differences and gross inequalities that affect women at the time when they would be pensionable.
I alluded a few moments ago to all the other differences that women have to face in employment, wage levels, services available to them if they have children they need to care for by themselves, discrimination in terms of housing accommodation, and so on. I mentioned earlier a few organizations which have done good work in this field. I should like to thank the Canadian Council on Social Development for a publication it put out recently giving statistics in all of these various areas affecting women. It is an interesting booklet. It probably came to all members as it came to me a few days ago. I recommend that hon. members study it. It is good for us to read this kind of material at a time when we are patting ourselves on the back and saying we are laying down in glowing language and in choice rhetoric that women are the equal of men in this country. Women may be the equal of men in constitutional terms, they may be equal before the law and before the courts; but in practical terms they are not. Why add to the difficulties that they face during their working years these inequalities which face them when retirement time comes?
There is one other piece of legislation I want to mention in this field the terms of which are probably contrary to one of the provisions in the bill now before us. I refer to the spouse's allowance. The minister says this is an equal piece of legislation, anybody, man or woman, can get that allowance between 60 or 65 provided he or she meets certain conditions. The conditions include two in the main. One is that you are married to and living with a spouse who is 65 or over. The other is that your means do not exceed a certain level. Therefore, it is equal. However, the fact is that women in that age

bracket who are in need but who are spinsters or widows do not qualify. Yet clause 17 of Bill C-25 provides:
The establishment of separate pension funds or plans for different groups of employees does not constitute the basis for a complaint under part III that an employer is engaging or has engaged in a discriminatory practice if the employees are not grouped in those funds or plans according to age, sex or marital status.
I suppose the "out" for the government on this is the reference to an employer. However, we are talking about pension plans. I submit that the spouse's allowance portion of the Old Age Security Act is directly contrary to something that is prohibited by this piece of government legislation in that persons are grouped according to age, sex or marital status. I submit that not only is this happening with the spouse's allowance contrary to the spirit and the letter of that law as I just read it, but that it is totally and grossly unfair.
That is, as I have indicated, the contribution I wanted to make to this debate. Like my friend, the hon. member for Greenwood, I do not like the provisions relating to the privacy commission set up by this bill. I think they are inadequate and can be dangerous. However, I do like the parliament of Canada enacting a law which declares:
-every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have-
Even if that is clumsy construction in our language, I am glad that it is spelled out as "he or she". It goes on, as my friend read it a moment ago:
-consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society, without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex or marital status, or conviction for an offence for which a pardon has been granted or by discriminatory employment practices based on physical handicap-
I am glad parliament is passing this; I am glad we are having this debate, standing up and expressing with great pride that we in Canada have come a long way. We have come a long way since Agnes MacPhail first stood in this House of Commons, the first woman to come here, and said that she asked for no quarter. We still have a long way to go. I am glad that other bodies such as those I have named are giving statistics and pointing out what needs to be done in areas of employment, housing, wage levels, availability of legal services, and all the rest.
I am grateful to you, sir, for letting me make the point this afternoon that we are a long way from equality of men and women in terms of pension rights. If this bill does not correct those rights, I hope we can at least persuade the government that when we have a statute that says these things about equality we ought to put them in effect. That will mean substantial amendments to the Old Age Security Act, the Pension Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act, the Public Service Superannuation Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Superannuation Act, the Canadian Armed Forces Superannuation Act, and quite a few others. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that parliament, having made this ringing declaration about equal rights, we will follow through with specific improvements. Let us make women equal, at least in pensions.
February 17, 1977

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was inspired by a number of statements in this debate which are worthy of the very best traditions of the House. I listened to some on the other side as well as some on this side. They show how fundamental, deep and very important this legislation is. As I listened to the proceedings in this chamber today I could not help but feel the importance of the matter raised by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) in the question period, the violation of human rights in Uganda, another part of the world. I want to associate myself with the matters he raised and the reply of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). We hope that legislation like this will make our country a much better place, and I am proud to support it.
Having said that, I want to refer to two clauses in the bill that give me a great deal of concern. I hope that some hon. members on the other side, especially the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), will give heed to what I have to say because I think I have an important point concerning this bill and other statutes. I refer to clauses 21 and 57. Let me quote from the statement made by the minister, as reported at page 2977 of Hansard of February 11, when he introduced this measure.
Enforcement of these and other provisions will be carried out under the proposed legislation by a human rights commission. The commission will have wide powers, including the power to establish tribunals able to impose severe financial penalty.
He went on to say:
As befits a body one of whose tasks will be to sit in judgment on government conduct, the human rights commission because, for example, of all the provisions which relate to the federal public sector as well as the private public sector, would, unlike those in some other jurisdictions, be independent of government and responsible only to parliament.
My concern is with regard to the proliferation of agencies and bodies responsible to parliament, and to the mechanism by which parliament exercises, or fails to exercise, jurisdiction. I hope that when the bill is referred to the committee hon. members will examine these clauses and, hopefully, modify some of them. Why should such a body report directly to parliament and not be responsible to the executive? The Advisory Committee on the Status of Women asked for it. The minister has told us that those who sit in judgment, as it were, on government conduct should report to parliament rather than to the executive. Mr. Speaker, we have heard this argument about independence a great many times. I maintain that the affairs of these bodies are conducted, not better but worse as a result of the absence of government supervision.
It is important that the executive arm of government assume responsibility not only for the matters raised by the Auditor General-and these are serious enough-but that it should answer for the policies carried out by independent agencies or bodies. The Auditor General tells us he cannot even supply a complete list of all the Crown corporations which exist. He appended a list to his report but he says he keeps finding new ones. I ask myself how many agencies report directly to
3153
Canadian Human Rights
parliament. The Auditor General does so himself, but he has a special committee of the House which considers his report; there is usually a standing reference giving the public accounts committee the responsibility of considering the report and calling the attention of the House and of the nation to the matters contained therein.
The Chief Electoral Officer is responsible only to parliament and the committee on privileges and elections usually assumes responsibility for dealing with the questions he raises. The Public Service Commission is similarly responsible only to parliament. The plight of the chairman of the Public Service Commission is something of a scandal. When the report of the Public Service Commission went before the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons almost two years ago, the chairman said, in effect, "Please, we want an examination of what is going on under the Public Service Employment Act". Eventually the government did make an announcement, some two weeks ago, that it would name a body whose duty it would be to carry out the inquiry requested. But there is no automatic referral to a committee of the report of the Public Service Commission.
The Commissioner of Official Languages reports to parliament and his work, too, is important. But which minister assumes responsibility for giving direction to him in terms of policy? My hon. friend might say a minister should not do that. The fact is, though, that there is no mechanism by which the House is exercising supervision, and I submit that when no effective supervision is exercised something unhealthy finally takes place. I call attention to the situation presented by the bill before us. Not only is the human rights commission responsible directly to parliament, but so is the privacy commissioner to be established under clause 57. He is a member of the human rights commission, but he has been given the responsibility of making a direct report to parliament.
I ask this question: what is the mechanism by which a member of this House can deal with one of these independent bodies? I do not know how many are on the list. The librarian of parliament is on it, and I am sure hon. members on reflection could add others who report directly to this place. Someone is going to say that the first thing that happens is the presentation of an annual report. Look at clause 47 dealing with the annual report; it states:
The commission shall, within five months after the 31st day of December in each year, transmit to the Minister of Justice a report of the activities of the commission under part II and this part for that year including references to and comments on any matter referred to in paragraph 22(1 )(e) or (0 that it considers appropriate and the minister shall cause the report to be laid before parliament within fifteen days after receipt thereof or, if parliament is not then sitting, on any of the first fifteen days next thereafter that parliament is sitting.
Earlier today I heard the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) ask the House leader to refer to a committee, as soon as possible, the government's estimates for expenditure in the coming fiscal year. The hon. member pointed out that there were only eight working weeks before the expiration of the time during which those estimates can be considered before the committee is required to report back. An annual report which need not be presented until the end of May will

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
always be more than a year in arrears when a committee comes to examine it, if it does at all.
Why should not this type of body report within 60 days of the end of the calendar year so that members might have an opportunity to examine it? On those rare occasions when those bodies appear before parliament, at least we would then have a current annual report before us. The suggestion that a body of this kind should have five months after the calendar year ended in which to present its report is an act of contempt of this place: it deliberately invites a situation in which members who try to interest themselves in what is taking place are unable to do so in any real sense.
I hope that when the bill goes to the committee it will be possible to reach general agreement to change clauses 43 and 60 which are parallel clauses. Five months is too long a period. There is no reason in the world why such an agency should not report by the end of February, thus giving parliament time to deal with any supplementary estimate if one were presented. Then the regular estimates would have some timeliness about them.
I should like to turn now to the question of appearance before committees. I know the standard answer of the ministry is, "Well, of course, you can always call people before a committee". But which committees, and how often? If an agency does something really wrong, the Auditor General will comment adversely and the matter will come before the public accounts committee. But how many of these independent agencies are called before the public accounts committee every year? I take my hat off to the current Auditor General who is looking hard at this area and especially at the operations of Crown corporations. He is doing a job which should have been done many years ago. What I am saying to hon. members is that we are adding two more bodies which will report directly to parliament and which will receive an absolute minimum by way of supervision.
What is the other mechanism by which such a body will come before parliament? It might appear at the time of the supplementary estimates which go before the miscellaneous estimates committee. Those of us who sat on that miscellaneous estimates committee know what a log-jam that is; everything is thrown at you. The steering committee meet and decide to call one or two, or perhaps a few more, of those particular agencies and groups who are especially interesting, but by no means do they call them all.
If there is no supplementary estimate, then the body does not even get called before that committee. Then we are dealing only with regular estimates, and the regular estimates are referred to any one of a number of committees of this House in the course of events. I suggest that the human rights commission might be called once every three or five years for half an hour before a standing committee of the House of Commons, and that is the degree of supervision that it is going to get. That is not good enough, Mr. Speaker.

I want hon. members of the House to think about this problem: how does parliament exercise supervision over this new family of agencies that we seem to be creating every week, which report directly to parliament when, in effect, parliament has no mechanism by which it exercises supervision? I suggest that there are worse things than having a minister responsible for such an agency-much worse things. If the agency were responsible to a minister, the minister would have to answer for it in the question period. He could not get up and say, "Well, that is an independent body and I am not responsible for it".
If it were responsible to a minister, Mr. Speaker, when the minister appeared before the committee dealing with his estimates or his supplementary estimates in every case members would have an opportunity to raise questions. It seems to me that the theory of responsible government is that the executive is responsible to the legislature. What we are trying to do is evade the very concept of responsible government itself, all in the name of virtue, all in the name of saying that we are creating something which is above and beyond parliament, so far beyond that the hands of politicians cannot touch it.
If we name bodies which are to be independent, immediately someone says, "Just like the judges are". But the judges are in a different position. The courts have a tradition and an established profession within the country that looks at everything they do. There are means by which those who are named to the bench and who fail to perform have to answer directly or indirectly. The independence of the judiciary is not in any way affected. I am suggesting that there are no comparable mechanisms in respect of this new family of agencies that we are creating if this bill is passed in the form in which it is presented to this House.
To me, one of the sadder things about Crown corporations- I see some other members here, such as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who are concerned about Crown corporations-is that they learned how to do things, such as setting up old boys' clubs, lunches, and so on. They get their estimates through and everything goes smoothly if it is done the right way. I would not suggest that perhaps the human rights commission should set up an old girls' club. Perhaps it would be nice if they could, but the number of women at the higher, responsible levels of the public service is so few that this is just not possible.
What is more than likely to take place, Mr. Speaker, if parliament does not consider this matter in some detail, is that we will create an agency which will manage to stay out of trouble and will not offend the Auditor General. It will avoid supplementary estimates and it will submit nice reports. It will conduct a few prosecutions, but not that many, and it will become an ineffectual body, in fact, escaping the immediate attention of anybody in terms of answering for its own actions. Mr. Speaker, I hope that this will not be the case.
I want to conclude by saying that I do believe in this bill. I think it is a tremendous bill. The principles behind it are very deep and profond, and in no way do I want what I have said to be a reflection on what the bill attempts to do. I have listened
February 17, 1977

to other members who have spoken from all parts of the House, and I know how deeply they feel about the bill. I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane), one of my colleagues, but with all due respect I could not agree with everything that he said. When I hear a member of a majority language group telling us what great rights the minorities have, I am always a little concerned, especially when the minorities come up to you and tell you that they do not have those rights.
I hope this bill will be passed and that the spirit that motivated it will be transformed into agencies which effectively can administer the bill. But I have major reservations about independent bodies which report directly to parliament, because I do not believe that parliament is equipped in the way in which it is structured and in the way the committee system functions, to give any supervision.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF INDIVIDUALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on a most vital subject, a bill that is, on the one hand, terribly important and, on the other hand, of such far-ranging scope and import that I fear it may be discussed in whispers and held up as something almost beyond criticism, when there are many penetrating questions to be asked about it on a whole variety of levels.
Whether one admires the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) or not, I do not think that the bill makes him the ombudsman, as someone recently said. In a way, I regret that the federal government has not moved to bring in that post and that individual, and I doubt whether the passage of this bill will in any way make unnecessary the role of ombudsman. I would hope that would still be considered and that that legislation will come before us very swiftly.
As the bill is spelled out, it is full of ringing words which have been mentioned by other speakers. For example, every individual should have an equal opportunity with other individuals to make for himself or herself the life that he or she is able and wishes to have, consistent with his or her duties and obligations as a member of society. One wonders whether that will end the closed shop, for example. This bill will have consequences which we cannot predict and interesting results will come from its passage. I, too, hope it will be passed and passed swiftly, but when some of its implications are fully understood I hope some of the people who are supporting the bill now will still support it.
The bill gives every individual equal opportunity without being hindered in or prevented from doing so by discriminatory practices based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, sex, marital status, or conviction for an offence in which a pardon has been granted, or by discriminatory employment practices. Brave words; noble words! The reference to "race" pleases me, because by passing this bill we should never again witness the experience of World War II when one particular racial group, or one part of a particular racial group, was singled out for one of the most serious discriminatory offences ever perpetrated by a government in this country. For Canadians of Japanese descent this bill, I
Canadian Human Rights
trust, will be seen as some guarantee to them, as something of their Magna Carta that nothing of that nature would be permitted or would be possible again in this country.
Mainly, I should like to concentrate on the aspects of the bill that deals with women's rights, with equality based on sex. I have heard people, both men and women, say to me within the past year, when talking about job mobility and professional access, that a woman can go as far as she wants if she wants to badly enough. I do not believe that at all. Men say it with pride; women say it with bravado. But we have not arrived at that situation yet.
I feel that there is a long way to go still, and I trust that the passage of this legislation will help. However, it will not be enough, and I suspect that one of the dangers in passing the bill is that some of the people who are prepared to fight the battle may feel that the battle is won. There are still areas of discrimination possible, and they are so subtle that the bill does not cover them. Let me give an example from outside the country. I attended for a year the Institute of Education in London, England, and while I was there the child development program was headed by an extraordinary woman who was remarkable in many respects. Yet she could never become a full professor because that department was not raised to a chair at the university. Eventually she retired and the post was filled by a man. Immediately afterwards it was constituted a chair and he became a professor at the university. How could anyone prove discrimination there? Everybody would have the finest regard for the work that Miss Gardner did throughout her years in that post, and I am sure that the senate and the board of governors would say that the elevation had nothing to do with the sex of the person filling the post. They would say it had everything to do with the new importance being attached to education, particularly to that branch of education.
There are areas of male dominance in this country, which the bill will be hard put to attack. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has referred to this chamber as being somewhat of a scandal in terms of the equality of women, if not of women's rights. Since the years when women were first permitted to vote and were first elected as members of parliament much progress has been made. But I wish he had mentioned some other great names, such as Ellen Fairclough, Mrs. Black, Tilly Rolston, and so on, and had broadened the catalogue a little by mentioning some of the people who established a role for women in the House in the pioneering days. Also, I should like to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for having appointed more than one woman to his cabinet. This is a great step at the federal level. At the provincial level, W. A. C. Bennett, when he was premier of British Columbia, took the revolutionary step of appointing three women at once to his cabinet.
Again, there are subtle areas of discrimination that are possible here and I felt that the cause of women's rights was set back a long way. I am referring to the time a couple of years ago when the main commissioner of the minister of

February 17, 1977
Canadian Human Rights
education of British Columbia was publicly fired by the premier on a television show when the minister was in Montreal. When she returned she did not resign immediately. The premier would not have been able to do that to a man. It would have been unheard of and unacceptable. Some of these things have to be fought at the highest level. One of these days I hope we will find a woman serving as a cabinet minister who will be prepared to resign if she felt she had not been treated properly, instead of accepting the situation. I wish the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mrs. Campagnolo) had not flirted with the idea of resignation in the last few days. It is part of the problem rather than part of the solution to one aspect of what can still be an area of discrimination.
As we go through the act, we find aspects of it that should be questioned. The bill goes beyond the traditional basis for discrimination, that is, colour, religion and national or ethnic origin, to include age. It is an interesting factor, not totally removed from the question of women's rights, and it is one of the great paradoxes in the country today because age will no longer be a factor in discrimination from birth onwards, but I gather it will still be a factor in the first nine months of life. Or does the passage of the bill mean that the practice of abortion will end in this country? Because there are racial groups in the country which count the age of the child at birth as being, the age of one. That is an interesting aspect of the hope that there will be no more discrimination on the grounds of age. It is a strange situation where life is preserved by statute.
Since we have abolished capital punishment it is difficult to take away a person's life without committing the crime of murder, yet it is possible to prevent some 50,000 Canadians from being born annually. That says something about this country, because I am sure that as soon as we have passed the bill many people will be applauding, clapping each other on the back and saying, "That is the kind of people we are who can pass this kind of legislation". But when we look at the statistics for abortion in this country, they also say something about the kind of society and the kind of people we are at present. There is a great paradox there which will be heightened rather than lessened by the passage of this statute.
I have been dealing with a private case which involves age and the way in which the government calculates it. I am awaiting the passage of this bill, following which I will raise it again with some of the officials of the Department of National Defence who will know what I am talking about. It involves the matter of a pension. There is certainly discrimination there because of what seems to me to have been an error made some years ago. It is one of the cases where the services of an ombudsman would be required. However, the passage of this bill might help to nudge the department into action or make possible the introduction of a private member's bill on this issue.
I am very interested in the question of equal pay for work of equal value. Here is a large area where women should benefit from this bill, although again we will have to know much more about the definition of "equal value". The principle would require employees to evaluate all jobs and determine pay rates
[Mr. Johnston.)
on the basis of skill, effort, responsibility and working conditions of each job. One suspects that there may well be too many loopholes there.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORTS OR REVIEWS RESPECTING NATIONAL FOOD POLICY
REQUEST FOR REPORTS OR REVIEWS RESPECTING NATIONAL FOOD POLICY
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for copies of any reports or reviews with respect to a national food policy prepared by or under the direction of the group known as the DMs Ten.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on November 24 I put down a notice of motion for the production of papers concerning the group known as DMs Ten and the reports or reviews which have been done for the cabinet. I did so for a number of reasons. First, I believe in openness in government, and when a group such as the DMs Ten prepares a paper with background on a possible food policy for this country I think that should be made available to the Canadian people so they can be part of the discussion of our food policy. I do not need to remind the House that this is national food week in Canada; the interest shown in it by people from coast to coast is evidence of the fact that they would like to participate in a national food policy.
Second, various parts of that document have been leaked to the press over the past seven or eight months, and without seeing the complete document there is a possibility of distortion. Unfortunately, this also creates in a community the pitting of producers against consumers and the building up of bogey men on both sides of the argument. When we draft a national food policy, we know that there will have to be some trade-offs between producers and consumers. These leaks have also had the effect of spreading certain rumours and creating hard feelings in the farm and consumer communities. I also have very strong suspicions that the discussion of a national food policy has caused sensitive feelings within the cabinet itself. I have the impression that there is an internal power struggle going on between the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), on one side, and other ministers such as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), on the other. I am asking the government to make public the DMs Ten report and all the background papers and study papers the DMs Ten looked at and made available to the cabinet, because I believe there should be openness. I believe the Canadian people should not be faced with a fait accompli and all of a sudden have a policy dumped upon them without their input.
I have before me a document which is alleged to be a copy of the DMs Ten report which was made to the cabinet on June 4, 1976. I want to spend what little time I have today referring to parts of that document which I have reason to believe is the report I am seeking in the House today. It is called "A Conceptual Framework for Food Policy in the Post-Controls Period". The object of the document is as follows:
This paper is intended to place before Ministers some of the elements at issue in the food sector and to obtain guidance as to the approach to be followed in the further elaboration of national food policy for the post-controls period.
National Food Policy
The introduction to the report reads in part as follows:
The first section, "Basic Food Policy Decisions", presents major questions (underlined for easy reference) on which officials feel they require guidance from Ministers prior to proceeding to draft, if they agree, a more definitive policy statement. The second section, "Conclusions", describes (in the interest of pointing out some practical results of the discussion) an outline of the elements of one possible food policy for Canadians in the post-controls period.
They go on to say:
Even though it would appear that the sufficiency of nutritional food supplies or the income-price relationship are not major issues facing consumers, one of the key requirements of a national food policy is maintenance of consumer confidence in the fairness and efficiency of the marketing system and of government policy in this area. In the same breath, the confidence of primary producers in a stable return on their large long-term investments in the relatively open agriculture and fishing industry must also be maintained.
After that they go on to outline some basic food policy decisions. I do not have time to cover those in detail, but they refer to the scope of a national food policy and what areas it should cover. They refer to the question of the role of market forces in a national food policy. They refer to trade and aid programs as they affect food. They refer to primary producers, the Fishermen and farmers of our country. They refer to processors, retailers and distributors in the food industry. They refer to consumer concerns and nutrition. When they talk about nutrition, they make the comment that Canada really provides very little to promote nutrition, and what we do provide as a nation is done in a very indirect way. They talk about the problems of federal-provincial relationships and they talk about the public information which should be part of a national food policy.
They go on to outline a possible food policy for Canada, and I gather this is what is being considered by cabinet ministers at this moment. I will read various parts of this document to the House. They begin by saying the following:
Canada's supplies of essential food products are adequate for the foreseeable future and there are resources to spare in some important areas. It would appear consumers need not worry unduly about the sufficiency of nutritional supplies. But, taking into account the world situation and the fact that Canadian agriculture and fisheries are open to the vagaries of climate, disease, etc ... . there is at once the opportunity to earn foreign currency (mostly through grains and fish), and the danger of excess pressure on domestic supplies and prices from abroad.
The policy of the federal government is, therefore, aimed at exploiting production strengths and moving into other effective areas of production in a consistent manner to ensure the adequacy of nutritional food supplies at competitive prices for the domestic market and for export.
The concentration of government efforts on those limited key areas where the consistent and balanced protection of the interests of all participants in the food marketing system is required and will have the desired result of:
(i)	shoring up consumer confidence in the fairness and efficiency of the
marketing system; and
(ii)	restoring producer confidence in a stable return on their large long-term
investment in the relatively open agricultural and fishing industries.
They then go on to outline various concerns with regard to a national food policy and they talk first of all about consumer concerns. This is where I have some questions, and I think many Canadians will have some as well. They say, first of all:
1.	The federal government recognizes that consumer interests must be given increased weight until there is a balance with the interests of producers in food policy formation and programs.
2.	The federal government rejects:

February 17, 1977
National Food Policy
(a)	statutory import quotas and tariffs providing relatively high or permanent protection (and, therefore, artificially high consumer prices) for some food products;
(b)	permanent or long-term consumer subsidies or two-price systems or export controls which can be expensive and distort the market, although short-term temporary subsidies might be effective for some basic commodities in specified situations.
3.	The federal government believes:
(a)	general income assistance programs already in place (U.I.C., pensions, indexing) are sufficient to provide average Canadians with the opportunity to eat in a nutritionally satisfactory manner;
(b)	the marginal or low-income consumer in Canada faces special income problems which will be solved by special means developed in the context of a social security review.
They go on to talk about the implications for action on these various consumer concerns, and here is where we get into some interesting debate. First of all:
Make administered pricing systems for dairy, eggs, poultry more compatible with consumer interests;
consumer representation on all national food boards or regulatory agencies-
When we start talking about issues like that, surely to goodness the government could at least allow a public debate before making decisions affecting the livelihood of many Canadians which would create a lot of acrimony in the community. The least we should ask for is a national debate. This report goes on to talk about the elimination of conflict of interest in the management of boards and agencies in these words:
-possible reorganization of departmental responsibilities. -Over a reasonable period of time, to review the import control list and all specific rates of duty on food products with a view to their eventual elimination;
-remove import ban on margarine;
-possible automatic destroy clause for Export and Import Permits Act with respect to need for individual import permits;
-eliminate two-price system for wheat-
It would be of considerable interest not just to producers but also to consumers if we were to eliminate the two-price system for wheat in this country. The other thing which I am sure would be shocking for consumers is the elimination of the skim milk subsidy and the comment about Canadians having adequate income assistance programs such as unemployment insurance, etc. They say this is in hand and we do not need any more revision of those areas. Then they talk about producer concerns and how government funds for investment in research and development of new and better varieties of product maintaining protein levels adaptable to Canada are needed. They go on to say that the federal government will work with the provinces in programs to preserve and promote a national market and that primary food production and its upgrading have been, and are, instruments of regional development.
Some of the implications of the producer concerns are: the total research and development outlay in Canada is $100 million, of which $70 million is salaries and wages; national

health and quality control programs are necessary; a national transport policy for foods for domestic use and export will be needed; we will also need an appropriate commercial policy, national income assurance programs, etc. Further on the memo refers to land use and the need to accelerate the national land use policy of this country. They refer to the need for amendments to the foreign investment review agency to accomplish those aims, and they say we need restrictions on foreign labour to encourage progress and mechanization in the agricultural field. Continuing with various producer concerns, the report talks about the need for a comprehensive production and marketing information system and the need for farm income stability. They seem to reject marketing boards as a form of income stability; the report seems to be geared toward lessening the influence of marketing boards.
They say that the general solution to income instability for average crop producers will involve crop insurance, income assurance plans of the producer-government contributory type, and income averaging annuities under the Income Tax Act. They make an interesting comment about the dairy industry, saying it is a special problem which in view of the $600 million treasury impact for the fiscal year 1976-77 has to be resolved in the context of the post-controls era, and that there should be a review of long-term dairy policy and possible federal-provincial financing of an independent inquiry into the industry.
On eggs and poultry, they say that a review of the acceptability of supply management-administered pricing under the auspices of a national farm products marketing act is required. There are a few other things they refer to which probably are not quite as important. Under the heading "Marketing", the report reads:
The federal government believes marketing boards are not synonymous with supply management or administered pricing and should not be used as instruments to stabilize or raise incomes directly. Some marketing boards have a positive impact on the food system, but their activities are in direct conflict with supply management mechanisms.
The federal government will work with the provinces to continue to minimize impediments to interprovincial flows of food products.
The federal government will work with foreign governments to reduce the international barriers to food trade.
They then suggest a whole series of implications in the area of export and import permits and the trade area. They suggest the need for reviewing, clarifying and possibly expanding the role of the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. I do not know what is happening about that in cabinet, but there was an interesting rumour about two weeks ago in one of the farm publications that the National Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act would be transferred to the jurisdiction of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. If that is the case, it is no wonder the Minister of Agriculture is becoming more and more grumpy when responding to questions in the House. There seems to be a conflict of opinion on marketing boards. The Minister of Agriculture is a staunch defender of them, but the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board has taken feed grains away from the authority of the Wheat Board, a move which concerns very many prairie farmers. It is good for the grain exchanges and for Cargill
February 17, 1977

Grain and all the corporations. Meanwhile, the Minister of Agriculture is saying that we need more orderly marketing. I wonder what the government's policy is.
I notice that the government leader in the Senate, Senator Ray Perrault, said during the Christmas holidays that he thought transport was too big a job for one minister and suggested it be divided. I suggest the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should begin the process by putting the Wheat Board under the authority of the Minister of Agriculture, where it belongs. I should like some clarification of the government's intentions in regard to marketing.
The memo goes on to discuss another very important aspect in part IV, under the heading "Processing, Distribution, Retailing Concerns". It says that some important market concentration and market power problems exist in Canada. That does not come as a great surprise. They talk about the implications of dealing with other problems concerning processing, distribution and retailing in the context of stage two of the Competition Act when it comes before parliament. The report says that the programs of incentives to enhance productivity and upgrading have been reviewed and that the federal government has directed that these programs be applied, on a priority basis, to the processing, distribution and retailing sector. They refer to the possibility of more incentive grants and more depreciation allowances as they affect retailing, processing and distribution in this country.
It is just about a year since the Food Prices Review Board reported that the retailing of food in this country is done by the large corporations which are very concentrated, and that as a result of lack of competition consumers pay more than they should. The government seems to imply they need more incentive grants and depreciation allowances in order to have a good food policy. I think we need an explanation of that, Mr. Speaker.
The memo says that the possibility of institutional change has been considered, but that the government does not believe that the creation of new institutions to deal with a food policy has a high priority. The formulation of policy and co-ordination of programs can be significantly improved without going the route of new institutions. It is said that the government has made certain decisions in this regard. Incidentally, this matter had led to conflicts within the cabinet, to some of those late-night quarrels one hears about between the Minister of Agriculture and other ministers.
I hope the government will make public the papers for which I am asking. I suggest that the Canadian people have the right to know. Various newspapers and members of the public have witnessed aspects of the DMs Ten-

speakeroldname: Mr. Ir6n6e Pelletier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORTS OR REVIEWS RESPECTING NATIONAL FOOD POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in all our discussions on a food policy, we should keep in mind that no two individuals, excluding groups and associations of any kind, think exactly the same way on this matter. As a matter of fact, it seems to me that we face a situation where we recognize some kind of failure in agriculture. The subject of a food policy for Canada comes up again and again. More than this, it is often brought up by people who do not know or prefer to ignore that the bases for such a policy have been established for some time and that they already operate effectively.
It might be worthwhile to recall that the idea of such a policy was brought forward eight years ago, namely in 1969. The prime objective of the Department of Agriculture which has been approved by cabinet, was and still remains to make agriculture in Canada an economically effective and independent industry. After further inquiries and several meetings and discussions, two special workshops were established in 1971. They had to determine the best ways to achieve these objectives. They made an excellent job and proposed the concept of a food system based on the market, and requiring therefore a good co-ordination between some 300,000 Canadian farmers and the various links of the food chain.
To meet the most essential food needs of Canadians, the farmer must not only be an efficient producer, but also be on very good terms with every level of his products marketing system-wholesalers, carriers, distributors retailers and, of course, consumers. Therefore this concept was shaped into a policy which is now working very well. Incidentally, there were four objectives reiterated in the Speech from the Throne of February 27, 1964.

Let me remind the House of these objectives. They were, first, to assure Canadians of high quality food at reasonable prices; second, to assure farmers a decent living; third, to provide food aid to countries where people cannot adequately feed themselves; and fourth, to produce products in which there would be a competitive advantage for domestic products for commercial export. In general terms, those objectives have been met, are being met and will continue to be met. They provide the broad basis for a food policy which makes Canada a world leader in this area.
In some countries farmers are making a hand-to-mouth living and food is cheap. In others, the farmers are on easy street but for the consumer the price of food is out of sight. A policy must maintain a balance between the primary producer and the consumer. That is what our policy is doing, and in response to changing times and patterns of consumerism it is changing and getting better all the time.
Look at the objectives one by one. The first, to assure consumers of a continuing supply of high quality food at reasonable prices, is one which, however successfully it may be realized, will constantly be taken for granted or overlooked by those who are quick to criticize. It is only taken for granted because it is working so well. When was the last time food was

February 17, 1977
National Food Policy
rationed in Canada? Not since World War II. If the average buyer found that the local supermarket was out of milk, meat, butter, vegetables, fruit or any of the 101 things we all take for granted, there might be some reason to get excited about a so-called new food policy. But because wide choice, high quality and stable prices are the norm, we all take food for granted. That would not be the case if, as happens in many countries, price, availability and quality were to fluctuate, or deteriorate as a result of a poorly organized agricultural industry. Canada's agricultural industry is probably the most efficient in the world. We do not have to import anything to keep ourselves well fed. We import because we want variety in our diets or because it makes economic sense, not because we need to import.
In the first objective high quality is mentioned. Mr. Speaker, Canadian food is the most wholesome anywhere, and our health and food inspection regulations help to keep it that way. The Department of Agriculture inspects and grades just about all the food we eat. The buyer knows, on buying it, not only that it is good to eat but how high is the quality of the food his or her food dollar is buying.
The first objective also makes certain that the food dollar is spread as far as it can go. Reasonable cost does not mean "cheap"; it means that food costs are maintained at reasonably stable levels in relation to producer-processor input and take-home pay. The average Canadian spends about one-fifth of his income on food, and the Americans-who are a little lower on that than we are-do not provide the same level of social assistance as we do in Canada. About 30 years ago a pound of butter cost just over an hour's wage-that is based on the minimum wage. Today, an hour's wage at the same level will buy you over two pounds; yet people complain that butter is being priced into the luxury class.
There is a popular notion that cheap food is a right. But why should one sector of society feed on the misery of another? If farmers are not given incentives to stay in business, to produce efficiently and at least earn a relevant return on their investment, there is no reason for them to consider staying in that line. If this country loses its farmers and relies on imports, the quality, abundance and, most importantly, price of food will change from one day to the next. We in this country will not be able to control those aspects; we will be too busy negotiating for sufficient quantities to feed our growing population.
That is where the second objective of the policy comes in. It assures the farmer of a decent living. But that does not mean that farmers benefit from an over-all security blanket. The assurance is there in the form of incentives and development programs for efficient farmers, but there is not too much for the farmer who will not keep up with the times. I do not see why farmers who are good at their job, who carry the multiple risks of their profession, who give the country its "staff of life", should be expected to take a loss and just survive. The rest of society expects a comfortable standard of living, modern conveniences, reasonable hours of work, educational and career opportunities for their children and the occasional holiday. Why should farmers have to take any less? The

commitment in terms of both money and time is a great deal larger in farming than for the average white collar or blue collar worker. Farmers should get the same return for their labour and investment as those in any other sector of the Canadian economy. If they find that they are at a dead end they are not going to encourage their children to follow their career path and they may very well quit themselves.
Farming is essential to this country. The food chain starts with the farmer. Food production has to be made attractive and kept stable if there are going to be farmers left on the land in Canada.
The third aim of the food policy is being achieved so successfully that, once again, not too many people bother to think about it. It is to provide food aid to the world's hungry population who cannot feed themselves. Canadians on a per capita basis are the biggest food donors in the world. We are the largest donor to the United Nations World Food Program in absolute terms. Our annual contributions for food aid are now up to $230 million.
Getting food accepted for food aid programs is not nearly as easy as it sounds. We simply cannot use food aid as a safety valve that we can turn on and off to deal with whatever surplus situation comes up. It has to be a product which can be used in recipient countries, which is acceptable given the dietary and religious restrictions prevalent in a country, and which is digestable given the diet patterns followed by the people in that country. That is not all.
Any food aid program has to take into consideration the economic stability of the food producers of a recipient region. There is no point in providing large quantities of a product which, in a short time, will be coming up for harvest from the country's own farmers. Whatever food aid we give must not interfere with the existing balance of their economy.
Lastly, the policy aims for an agricultural industry that can export food to earn foreign currency. Income from exports is what keeps the economy healthy. In 1975 agricultural exports amounted to approximately $2.9 billion.
All the four objectives are being achieved, but to keep the agricultural food relationship a happy and a productive one it is only reasonable to look to the start of the food chain to see what can be done to make sure that the supply does not dry up.
Farmers look for income stabilization, they look for some sort of power to take on the corporate giants which can effectively hold their industry to ransom. With the introduction of marketing boards, backed by both federal and provincial governments, they have, in many cases, the edge they need. Government programs through the Agricultural Stabilization Board have helped maintain the farm price for many products. Recent legislative changes have expanded the number of protected products, and increased the flexibility of support to farmers.

February 17, 1977
Agriculture Canada backs the Canadian farmer not only with hard cash, but with a variety of programs designed to give him the resilience and ability to stay in business.
Such things as production research, inspection and grading of commodities, market information and protection of animal health go to strengthen the farmer's competitive position. Crop insurance, compensation programs for lost livestock, and development of hardy, disease resistant strains help protect the farmer against natural hazards.
The Canadian Dairy Commission, the National Farm Products Marketing Council, the Agricultural Stabilization Board, the storage assistance program are examples of some of the tools the farmer has working for him when it comes to fighting the effects of short-term market distortions. Agricultural markets are constantly being explored, extended, and often improved by the work of such government sponsored agencies as the Canadian Grain Commission and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board.
All in all, this government is proud of the food policy platform it has laid down, and made to work over the years. Unfortunately, as I have said before, the reason that it has been ignored is simply because it has worked so well. That is not to say that the policy is conclusive. Exactly the reverse is the case. We have a base on which we can build, and this is happening all the time. Any policy, to remain current and relevant, must keep up with changing times. Our present policy is no different. To make it relevant with the context of today, and keep it that way for tomorrow, it must be constantly reviewed, renovated, adapted and expanded.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose that in doing so one should take criticism into consideration. Besides, coming from those who know the facts and the problems, criticisms are often a positive element. But from those who understand nothing of the problem, who only want to make headlines and who are constantly on the look-out for leading causes, that is another matter.
I am always surprised to see how often media give special recognition to subjects related to food policy. But again, I must recall that headlines seldom reflect reality. It is not unusual to see big red headlines which fade out or are shelved for good when it comes to facts. In this day and age, with all that gibberish about food policy, some think that the situation is definitively dreadful. It is most unfortunate since changing for the sake of it might bring us to an even worse situation.
The principles of the present policy are entirely logical and quite useful for all Canadians. However, they are constantly questioned. It is absolutely necessary to update it constantly and remove the weakest points as soon as they are detected. The consumer must be assured of the best value possible for each dollar allotted for food. The farmer must increase his efficiency through marketing procedures, processing costs established in relation to the cost of the finished product and he must be very closely supervised. Agriculture, Mr. Speaker, is closely connected with each of the numerous links in the food chain. There is plenty of room for various programs meant to improve the process.
National Food Policy

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORTS OR REVIEWS RESPECTING NATIONAL FOOD POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to contribute a few words to this debate as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
National Food Policy

Consumers in Canada are becoming more and more concerned about food. In recent years they have seen people in countries overseas suffering from food shortages or famines. Canada is one of the world's main agricultural exporting nations. They wonder how she can help to reduce these shortages. Some even wonder if Canada itself might be facing food shortages some time in the future. They realize, of course, that there is little or no chance of that happening today.
The consumer has had to accept higher prices for food in recent years. Indeed it is fair to say that consumer interest in a national food policy is due directly to the food price explosion of 1972 and 1973. Between 1971 and 1975 food prices rose by about 60 per cent. By contrast, prices of all goods and services as measured by the consumer price index increased less than 40 per cent. The higher food prices are a burden to low income Canadians. Many Canadians cannot afford to eat well, even though they may be spending 40 per cent of their income on food. It is true that food prices did not increase through 1976. An increase of 1.2 per cent in January, 1977, coming after a small increase in December, 1976, seems to show that the upward trend may be back with us again.
Consumers are also concerned with what they are eating. They worry about the long-term effects of the many chemicals that are added to processed foods. They see children and teenagers eating junk foods. They know that many Canadians are poorly fed. Others-as one sees all too often-are eating too much. A shortage of essential foods and an excess of others can cause health problems or even death for the individuals concerned. This adds to the cost of our health programs.
Finally, consumers are questioning some of the marketing practices and power of the large food chains. As is well known, a few firms dominate the food retailing system. Consumers question why prices seem to vary from store to store for no obvious reason. They wonder how much all the promotions, "free" offers and advertising add to food costs. They feel that the food they buy lacks quality. In short, consumers are losing confidence in the food system. This explains why they are so interested in having a national food policy in Canada.
A food policy is of vital concern for Canada. We need a national food policy no less than we need a national energy or transportation or defence policy. Such a policy must be an integrated one. It must cover all parts of the food system. It should reflect the very real concerns of consumers. It should also respond to matters of concern to agriculture and farmers. It should be concerned with the industries which provide farmers with their fertilizers, chemicals and machinery. It should relate to the industries which process and distribute to consumers food products after they have left the farm.
In our food policy we must be fair to consumers. Some people think that a few of the farm programs we now have may result in higher costs for consumers. These are programs which stabilize and support farm prices and incomes. Marketing boards are a good example. It is important, however, to distinguish between different types of marketing boards. Some of them negotiate contracts on behalf of producers, others

assemble and offer products for sale. There is no quarrel here. There are other boards which have the power to set prices. They may also control the quantity which is produced. They may even control imports as well. It is these boards that people are worried about. Perhaps we should consider if there are other ways of achieving stability in agriculture that avoid giving monopoly powers to producer groups.

Mr.Speaker, when I commenced my remarks this afternoon I mentioned that people sometimes say that we have advanced to the point where a woman can reach any objective that she sets for herself if she wants to get there badly enough. I do not think that is the case. In fact I am inclined to believe, if I may paraphrase the remarks of a former mayor of this city, that a woman has to work twice as hard to get half as far.
I find myself interested in the principle of equal pay for work of equal value. Probably one of the most important phrases in the entire bill is "work of equal value," and I hope we will see the day when the underpaid feminine secretary who is running the whole show, turning any profits that may be turned, and holding the entire thing together, at a salary a fraction of the person's who is the titular head of the organization, will receive a remuneration equivalent to the value of the work that she is doing for the business or the profession in which she works. It is only then that we will have taken a great step forward. It is interesting to note that if women actually achieve that and are paid equal pay for work of equal value,

then the goal set by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) of seeing a greatly enlarged number of women in this Chamber will not be met simply because to get here politically-and the law will not change that in any way-a woman still has to be twice as good and work twice as hard. Of course the representation that we have here is remarkable.
One of the things that most encourages me about the potential success of the bill is the way in which the women's movement in the last 10 or 15 years in North America has forced changes in the languages so that one must be very careful now. I was speaking at an inaugural session of the city council in my constituency during the Christmas break. It is a council which at present, regrettably, has no women on it at all. I was making a run-through of other towns and municipalities in my constituency, pointing out the women who had been elected or re-elected aldermen and mayors in those communities, and I almost fell into the trap of describing them as able and charming, or able and beautiful. Then I realized that one would not describe a male alderman that way and that I had better be circumspect in my language, so I was reduced to describing them simply as able. That adjective certainly can be applied to the women representatives that we have here in parliament. They have come through a finer screen than any of the men who are here in order to be representatives, but when they go out to their constituencies advising the sisterhood to run for office, they are going to be told by those sharp business people that when the pay scale is considered, there is not enough in it. If women are going to get equal pay for work of equal value, the pay scale would not tempt people to come here, so I suspect the bill will not advance the cause which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre put forward so ably and excellently as long as the pay scale for a member of parliament is as uncompetitive as it is with anything equivalent anywhere else in the business or professional field in this country. However, I hope that can be changed.
I find the little exception with regard to age and retirement to be interesting. I suspect that will be one of the first clauses of this bill to be appealed because we are approaching the time when this business of automatically retiring at an earlier and earlier age will be challenged, and that will be seen in the not too distant future as a discrimination which cannot be tolerated. I think it would help women most of all if there was a flexible retirement age because I have seen too many who, by the time they are 55 or so, Find that they can no longer attain any employment, and at that time they have to go on welfare. It would be more practical if they could retire on a pension at that time, if they should choose to do so, and if others, along with males who are vigorous at 65, could continue for somewhat longer if they should wish to do so. I suspect that we will have to move to something of that nature following passage of this bill.
One of the regrettable aspects of our times is the increased crime rate, but this bill excludes inmates who have served their sentences. It protects a person who is granted a pardon as if his
February 17, 1977

crime had never been committed, and he is totally absolved of it, but one despairs for a country which will not accept the rehabilitating nature of a prison sentence, nor even the punishment aspect of it.
One of the reasons we have a parliamentary committee touring this country is to see what is wrong with our prisons. One of the things which is wrong is that almost everyone in them knows that after the sentence has been served a person has to pay and pay for the rest of his or her life. There is a discrimination there because we do not basically believe that a person has paid for his crime when he has finished his sentence. I realize how very difficult it would be, however, to extend this clause further than it goes at the present time.
There are important questions we could ask about the commission and its power to turn away a complainant if it thinks the problem can be solved elsewhere. If the commission refuses to hear a case, there is no provision for appeal, and people would then be thrown back on their own resources to the courts or other agencies. Whether there should be some check on the power of the commission in that way, I suppose we will have to wait and see. We will have to wait to see what regulations will govern its operation.
I realize that there are many things which bother the Advisory Council on the Status of Women about this bill. One prime objection is the exclusion of protection for Indian women against the discrimination which exists and which is embodied in the Indian Act. On this aspect the bill as it stands is no help at all. I do not think we should leave a growing portion of the population outside the law. There should be equal rights across the country.
I think we should seriously consider the Indian Act as it relates to this human rights bill because we cannot say that our aboriginal people are any less worthy of equal treatment in these areas.
We need some concrete suggestions as to the standards of skill, effort, responsibility, and conditions of work. The proposed human rights commission should establish effective standards to define these matters clearly so that we will know what they are, and so that the mass of litigation and appeals to the commission can be reduced. One would hope that that would serve a persuasive purpose in terms of hiring practices. Unless there is some definition or some guideline clearly set out, then the proposed human rights commission will be more swamped than the Anti-Inflation Board has been, and it will have to take unto itself a staff of enormous size in order to deal with the multitude of complaints which I am sure will be presented.
I hope that when this bill becomes law there will not be very many parts of it which will be disallowed or found to be inoperative because changes were not made in the Interpretation Act, and again the proposed human rights commission should concern itself with monitoring all the legislation which has been passed which has made it difficult for women to have their rights upheld in the courts.
Canadian Human Rights
I recommend for anyone's reading an article by Marguerite E. Ritchie entitled "Alice Through the Statutes" which appears in the McGill Law Journal, volume 21, No. 4 of the winter of 1975. That was not very long ago, and yet the writer found it necessary to sound a warning about the inability of women to find that they can be given the rights which are assumed to exist for men. I know that the bill before us refers to an individual; it does not use the word "male". The bill assumes that women have the same rights, so that may be taken care of, but I hope the minister will address himself to the concerns which have been presented to me by women who have had lengthy experience in Ottawa and who are familiar with some of the difficulties involved in taking a case to court in an attempt to remove discrimination.
The closing words of Marguerite E. Ritchie's article are interesting, and I quote:
For over a hundred years it has been clear that legislation drafted in terms of the male exposes women to denial of rights granted to men. Even legislation drafted in neutral terms has often been used to exclude women from rights and privileges. The whole structure of the law with respect to women rests upon judgments of men who regarded women as inferior. Women who seek even the smallest hope of equality must demand express legislation, written in the clearest possible terms. Yet legislation, however clear, has often failed at the hands of antagonistic male judges.
What is the answer? What should women and those men who sympathize with them do? Would it be better to ignore the Interpretation Act and to concentrate on other statutes which appear to promise equality? Will the promise of these statutes be any better than the illusion of the Interpretation Act?
Examples are cited with regard to the failure of that act to protect, and finally, in conclusion, the writer says this:
What we do know is that words can be made to mean many different things. It all depends on who is drafting the statutes and who is deciding upon their meaning.
Lewis Carroll said it all in "Alice Through the Looking Glass":
"When I use a word," Humpty Dumpty said, in rather a scornful tone, "it means just what I choose it to mean-neither more nor less."
"The question is," said Alice, "whether you can make words mean so many
different things."
"The question is," said Humpty Dumpty, "which is to be master-that's
all."
And that is the question. Not for dogs and cats, but for women and men who are concerned about something called justice.
As we prepare to pass this bill in which we can all agree with so much, there are still questions to be raised. I do not think there is anyone here so optimistic he would not see the bill failing to take its full effect until it has been used and faced with the challenges that will inevitably arise and which must be carried through to the Supreme Court of Canada for the final decision on whether the bill truly achieves the high aims set out in its magnificent and revolutionary preamble.
If I might make a final point, it is that this bill will be distinctively Canadian in its scope compared to practically every other nation in the world. We will have something that many people who come to this country will not have experienced in other parts of the world-a kind of freedom, a kind of mobility in the society forecast in these bright areas that I hope we can achieve. But we must realize that there are

many countries in the world that, by their very nature and their long history, have not provided equality on all of these bases the way this bill will do for this country. We will be moving into a class that is distinct, separate, and special.
It will be to the credit of this country to pass the bill, but we must be warned that the struggle is not over the moment the legislation is proclaimed. It will have to be monitored by every group interested in preventing discriminatory practices whether by race, ethnic origin, colour, sex or marital status. Only by that kind of eternal vigilance can it be made part and parcel of our life and culture, something which we accept and in which we believe.
